name: Lymphatic drainage facial massage
lead: Lymphatic drainage facial massage is a light, rhythmic, hands-on or tool-assisted massage of the face and neck meant to move lymph fluid, with the aim of reducing puffiness and giving a more defined, 'depuffed' look, particularly around the eyes, cheeks and jaw. It draws on manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), a gentle skin technique developed in the 1930s.[1][2]

People do it in the morning or before events for a slimmer-looking, more awake face, using hands, rollers or gua sha-style tools. Facial gua sha surged on TikTok in 2021 and 2022 as influencers promoted it for lymphatic drainage and refreshed-looking skin.[3] Plastic surgeon Jennifer Levine told The List that massage may reduce puffiness by moving lymph fluid, though the effect is temporary.[2] Dermatologist Michael Detmar said promoting lymphatic flow can have benefits, noting that ageing and sun damage can reduce the skin's lymphatic vessels.[2]

Dermatologist George Cotsarelis has said that people without facial lymphatic problems would not benefit.[2] The research base for MLD itself centres on lymphedema, and no published trial of facial lymphatic massage for cosmetic depuffing has been found.[1]

paras: Manual lymphatic drainage applies very light pressure, under roughly 4 kPa, in rhythmic circular strokes, and is described as distinct from conventional massage. It rests on the idea that gentle skin movement can encourage lymph to drain from tissues; lymph itself moves through contractions in vessel walls and through skeletal muscle movement [1]. Facial versions apply similar strokes toward the neck and collarbone area, and are also sold in the form of rollers, gua sha-style tools and devices. The List describes MLD as light pressure with pumping and circular motions along the lymph channels.[2] Wikipedia notes that practitioners use lighter pressure for cosmetic facial gua sha than for muscle or joint work, with tools such as jade stones and ceramic spoons and an oil or balm on the skin.[3]

Danish doctors Emil and Estrid Vodder developed the technique in the 1930s. Working on the French Riviera with patients who had chronic colds, they noticed swollen lymph nodes and began developing light rhythmic hand movements in 1932, introducing the technique in Paris in 1936 and later training practitioners in Copenhagen after World War II [1]. Its adoption as a beauty practice and its spread through social media are not documented in the sources reviewed.

MLD is presented mainly as a treatment for lymphedema, including after breast cancer. Results are described as mixed. A 2013 systematic review of breast cancer-related lymphedema found no clear support for MLD in either preventing or treating limb swelling, while a 2022 study of 80 patients with lower-limb lymphedema reported an increase in opened lymphatic pathways [1]. These findings concern limb lymphedema, not facial cosmetic use.

Levine told The List that there is anecdotal evidence that fluid returns after massage, that she does not recommend post-surgery lymphatic massage herself though some therapists do, and that she considers it unnecessary but not harmful to healing.[2] Detmar said a facial that encourages drainage might reduce fluid build-up.[2] Cotsarelis called such facials useless for people without lymphatic problems.[2]

The List identifies no significant risks of lymphatic facial massage, and Levine says it is not detrimental to healing.[2] Gua sha tools used with firmer, scraping strokes nearly always cause minor skin trauma such as redness or bruising, according to Wikipedia, which also lists rarer harms and says infection is a concern if tools are not sterilised.[3]
No studies found on facial lymphatic massage for cosmetic depuffing or skin tone. Studies of manual lymphatic drainage in lymphedema exist but are a different condition and are mixed in outcome [1].

timeline.event: Emil and Estrid Vodder begin developing light rhythmic hand movements [1]

card.summary: Gentle face and neck massage meant to depuff; the technique is real, but cosmetic facial evidence is absent.
card.aka: Facial MLD, face lymph massage, depuffing massage
card.note: Evidence for MLD is in lymphedema, not facial cosmetic use.

quick.overview:
Lymphatic drainage facial massage uses very light strokes on the face and neck to encourage fluid movement, with the aim of reducing puffiness.

The parent technique, manual lymphatic drainage, dates to 1930s Europe and is studied for lymphedema with mixed results. Facial cosmetic use has not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say light rhythmic pressure helps lymph flow away from swollen tissue. Light-pressure MLD is the technique reported in the lymphedema literature.
quick.risks: No facial-specific safety data were found. The sources reviewed do not discuss contraindications.

chain: Light strokes move fluid toward the neck and collarbone
Temporary puffiness around the eyes, cheeks and jaw reduces
Face looks more defined and awake for a time
angle.text: People use facial lymphatic massage for a short-term depuffing effect, typically in the morning or before photos and events. Surgeon and dermatologist comments describe the benefit as real but temporary.
